## Paper

## Abstract

While extensive efforts have been devoted to enhancing electron transfer efficiency through metal valence cycling in heterogeneous Fenton-like reactions, the potential catalytic improvement induced by dynamic structural stretching remain unexplored. Here, we introduce a homointerpenetrated Fe-based metal‒organic framework (BUC-95) featuring a dynamic stretchable structure that significantly boosts the heterogeneous Fenton-like catalytic performance. BUC-95’s unique stretchable structure achieved effective peroxydisulfate activation for degrading various micropollutants via Fe(IV)=O species, facilitated by a reduced energy barrier for Fe(IV)=O formation through modulation of the electron density at Fe sites. DFT calculations suggest that, compared with the isostructural analogue with hydrogen bond-restricted stretching, the flexible dynamic stretching in BUC-95 overcomes the inherent electron transfer limitations from Fe sites to peroxydisulfate, enhancing the ofloxacin degradation performance. Practically, BUC-95 demonstrated effective continuous-flow degradation and detoxification of micropollutants. This work establishes dynamic stretching as a crucial design principle for advancing environmental remediation materials and technologies.

---

## Introduction

Fenton-like reactions have been extensively employed to degrade emerging refractory contaminants in wastewater. These reactions leverage the ability of oxidants such as hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), peroxydisulfate (PDS), and peroxymonosulfate (PMS) to form diverse reactive oxygen species (ROSs) through activation processes1–5. During the reaction process, the efficiency of electron transfer from catalytic sites to the oxidants plays a critical role, as it directly governs the productivity and speciation of ROSs6,7. Extensive research efforts have been devoted to designing heterogeneous catalysts from micron to atomic scales8,9 to increase electron transfer kinetics through strategically modulating the electronic microenvironment surrounding catalytically active sites10–13. Nevertheless, the inherent complexity of interfacial reaction dynamics frequently induces transient structural evolution in catalysts, a phenomenon often overlooked in conventional studies but capable of exerting profound implications on the overall catalytic oxidation mechanisms14–16.

A few recent research efforts have focused on elucidating the critical role of dynamic structural distortion in modulating the local coordination environment of metal sites during catalytic processes. For example, it was reported that the interaction between host and guest molecules might induce the stretching vibrations of O‒Sr‒O and Co/Ti‒O bonds within the Co/La-SrTiO3 catalyst to increase electron transfer efficiency from PMS to metal sites16. However, the current understanding remains constrained by two fundamental limitations: (1) the catalytic performance improvement achievable through stretching vibrations of metal‒oxygen bonds is inherently limited because of the insufficient structural adaptability of conventional catalysts; and (2) the development of synthetic strategies for engineering catalysts with programmable dynamic stretching architectures presents technical challenges, particularly in advanced oxidation processes. More importantly, the relationship between the structural dynamic stretching of catalysts and the resulting catalytic activity remains poorly defined.

Interpenetrated metal‒organic frameworks (MOFs) offer a promising paradigm for addressing these challenges. Characterized by mutually entangled yet noncovalently bonded identical networks17,18, these architectures might exhibit intrinsic structural flexibility derived from the tunable spatial separation between constituent frameworks. This unique structural feature enables reversible deformation of the entire framework in response to external stimuli like chemical activation. Unlike the localized pore breathing in conventional MOFs or the ligand-based flexibility in flexible MOFs (Supplementary Fig. 1), the large-scale dynamic adaptability of interpenetrated MOFs make them ideal model systems for studying whole-framework dynamics in Fenton-like reaction mechanisms.

In this work, a homointerpenetrated MOF (denoted BUC-95, CCDC:2352385) with a dynamically stretchable framework was synthesized, which exhibited exceptional degradation efficiency for diverse organic contaminants through a high-valent iron-oxo (Fe(IV)=O)-dominated oxidation pathway. Experimental characterizations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that the presence of hydroxylated BUC-95 not only regulated the d-orbitals electron density of Fe but also greatly reduced the activation energy barrier, promoting the formation of Fe(IV)=O in the BUC-95-OH/PDS system. Compared with the homointerpenetrated BUC-96 counterpart with restricted dynamic stretching, the flexible dynamic stretchability of the homointerpenetrated BUC-95 framework overcame the limitation of weak electron transfer performance in PDS activation processes to ultimately improve the catalytic ofloxacin (OFC) degradation performance. Furthermore, the construction of a fixed-bed continuous-flow catalytic reactor and tests with multiple toxicity assessment systems confirmed the stable long-term catalytic activity and exceptional detoxification capabilities of the BUC-95/PDS system. This work provides insight into the design and preparation of interpenetrated MOFs with dynamic stretching features for highly efficient water purification via Fenton-like reactions.

---

## Results

Characterization and structural analysis
BUC-95 was synthesized from FeSO4·7H2O, 4,4′-bipyridine (bpy) and 1,4-benzenedicarboxylic acid (H2bdc) via a facile microwave-assisted method (Supplementary Fig. 2). According to scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Supplementary Fig. 3) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) (Fig. 1b) analysis, BUC-95 exhibited a rod-like morphology, with particles sized ~15.0μm×1.0μm×0.3μm. The small size of the particles rendered the conventional single-crystal X-ray technique unsuitable, so microcrystalline electron diffraction (microED) was employed to acquire single-crystal data19,20. The crystal structure was determined ab initio from the microED dataset using the SHELX software package21 (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). The 3D reconstructed reciprocal lattice (Fig. 1a) obtained via microED revealed that BUC-95 (molecular formula Fe4(bpy)4(bdc)4) crystallizes in a triclinic unit cell with a = 11.490(2) Å, b = 16.460(3) Å and c = 21.183(4) Å and belongs to space group P1. BUC-95 features a homointerpenetrated structure consisting of a pair of identical 3D frameworks. The framework contains paddle-wheel-type binuclear Fe units, where each Fe atom is coordinated by four oxygen atoms from COO– groups of three deprotonated bdc2− ligands and two nitrogen atoms from two bpy ligands, forming a 3D framework (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 4).

The experimental powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns showed strong agreement with the simulated profiles derived from crystallographic data determined via microED, thereby confirming the phase purity of the as-synthesized BUC-95 (Fig. 1e). This finding was also confirmed through HR-TEM (Fig. 1d), elemental mapping (Supplementary Fig. 5), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Supplementary Fig. 6), Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) (Supplementary Fig. 7)22, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) (Supplementary Fig. 8), and elemental analyses (Supplementary Table 3).

To elucidate the role of dynamic stretching in BUC-95, BUC-96 (CCDC: 2263764) (Supplementary Fig. 9) was synthesized as an isostructural analog for comparison23. In BUC-96, H2bdc was replaced with 2,5-dihydroxyterephthalic acid (H4dhtp). Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) data revealed that BUC-96 adopts a homointerpenetrated 3D framework, in which Fe sites are coordinated with four oxygen atoms from three partly deprotonated H2dhtp2− ligands and two nitrogen atoms from two bpy ligands (Supplementary Fig. 10). It was observed that N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) molecules were encapsulated within the channels of BUC-96, where the O atoms from DMF form hydrogen bonds (2.509 Å) with hydrogen atoms from bpy ligand. These interactions almost completely restrict the dynamic stretching behavior inherent to the homointerpenetrated framework (Supplementary Fig. 11 and Supplementary Video 1). Additionally, the independent gradient model (IGM) visualization further demonstrated strong hydrogen-bonding interactions (represented by blue isosurfaces) between the DMF molecule and bpy ligands24 (Supplementary Fig. 12).

As depicted in Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 13, the X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) data and corresponding fitted information indicated that the valence state of Fe ranged between +2 and +3 in BUC-95 and BUC-96. This observation aligns with the Fe 2p XPS spectra (Supplementary Fig. 14). Additionally, a distinct positive shift (ca. 0.35 eV) in the Fe K-edge and the increased intensity of the whole O K-edge (Supplementary Fig. 15) were observed for BUC-95 compared with BUC-96, indicating a lower electron density at the Fe and O centers in BUC-9525. Extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra confirmed that the Fe atoms in BUC-95 and BUC-96 were six-coordinated by four O atoms from bdc2− or H2dhtp2− and two N atoms from bpy ligands (Fig. 1g). In particular, the EXAFS results revealed that the average lengths of the Fe‒O and Fe‒N bonds in BUC-95 were 2.402 Å and 2.255 Å, respectively (Supplementary Table 4), which are comparable to those of the Fe‒O (1.98 Å ~ 2.402 Å) and Fe‒N (2.14 Å ~ 2.255 Å) bond obtained from microED. The wavelet transform (WT) (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 16) plots revealed a clear intensity feature at ca. 3.0 Å−1 corresponding to Fe‒O/N coordination shells in both BUC-95 and BUC-96, whereas the absence of characteristic Fe‒Fe scattering paths at ca. 7.0 Å−1 excluded Fe‒Fe bonds.

Catalytic performance and preliminary mechanism
To systematically assess the Fenton-like catalytic efficiency of BUC-95 across various oxidant systems, ofloxacin (OFC), a representative fluoroquinolone antibiotic, was selected as the model contaminant. BUC-95 demonstrated superior peroxydisulfate (PDS) activation capability, achieving >99.99% OFC removal within 10.0 min, accompanied by an exceptional pseudo-first-order rate constant (kobs) of 5.52 min−1 (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 17). This performance surpassed those in different systems like BUC-95/PMS (81.4% removal, 2.94 min−1), BUC-95/H2O2 (86.6% removal, 3.46 min−1), conventional homogeneous Fe(II)/PDS (13.0% removal, 0.37 min−1) (Supplementary Fig. 18). And it also exceeded other MIL-based systems like MIL-88A(Fe)/PDS (41.2% removal, 0.82 min−1), MIL-88B(Fe)/PDS (41.7% removal, 0.83 min−1), MIL-88C(Fe)/PDS (48.43% removal, 0.94 min−1), MIL-53(Fe)/PDS (46.23% removal, 0.90 min−1), MIL-100(Fe)/PDS (41.96% removal, 0.73 min−1) and MIL-101(Fe)/PDS (54.46% removal, 0.79 min−1) by 1.88-fold, 1.60-fold, 14.9-fold, 6.73-fold, 6.65-fold, 5.87-fold, 6.13-fold, 7.56-fold and 6.99-fold, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 19 and 20), which was further supported by the normalized results based on BET surface area and Fe content between MIL-based catalyst and BUC-95 (Supplementary Fig. 21 and Supplementary Table 5).

DFT calculations were applied to investigate the difference in the activation process of PDS, PMS and H2O2 on BUC-95. Computational modeling of the adsorption configurations revealed distinct binding energetics: PDS exhibited the most favorable adsorption energy (Eads = −6.95 eV) on BUC-95, followed by H2O2 (−4.94 eV) and PMS (−2.16 eV) (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 22). Bader charge analysis was applied to quantify the interfacial electron transfer, revealing that 1.6437 e⁻ were transferred from BUC-95 to PDS, which was greater than those to H2O2 (1.0452 e⁻), and PMS (1.0367 e⁻) (Supplementary Fig. 23). These results collectively confirmed that PDS is the thermodynamically preferred oxidant activated by BUC-95.

The BUC-95/PDS system exhibited a 2.3-order-of-magnitude increase in reaction rate (kobs = 5.52 min−1) compared with that of its structural analog BUC-96 (kobs = 0.03 min−1, Fig. 2c), suggesting that the flexible dynamic stretching of the homointerpenetrated BUC-95 framework may substantially enhance the catalytic performance compared with the BUC-96 with restricted stretching induced by hydrogen bonding interactions.

Additionally, broad-spectrum degradation capability was validated for diverse contaminants, like enrofloxacin (ENR, kobs = 6.50 min−1), norfloxacin (NOR, 8.61 min−1), ciprofloxacin (CIP, 9.96 min−1), tetracycline (TC, 9.98 min−1), and diclofenac (DCF, 9.95 min−1), with performance exceeding that of other catalysts by 1~3 orders of magnitude (Fig. 2d, e, Supplementary Fig. 24 and Supplementary Table 6), which were consistent with the electrostatic potential (ESP) results. Nearly 100% OFC degradation efficiency and minimal Fe leaching (<1.5 mg L−1) after ten operational cycles demonstrated the robust reusability and stability of BUC-95 (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. 25), which were confirmed by the SEM images and PXRD patterns of the BUC-95 after five and ten cycles (Supplementary Fig. 26). BUC-95 maintained robust catalytic performance under a low PDS dosage (0.35 mM) across a wide pH range (2.5~8.5) (Supplementary Fig. 27), demonstrated strong resistance to multiple anions (Cl−, SO42−, NO3−, HCO3−) and humic acid (HA) (Supplementary Fig. 28), and performed effectively in complicated aqueous matrices like tap water, lake water, and rainwater (Supplementary Fig. 29). These results collectively suggest that nonradical oxidation pathways might dominate the degradation process. The addition of Cl− resulted in only minor inhibition of OFC degradation (<13.0% decline), which could be attributed to the competitive consumption of a few active species to form less reactive chlorine radicals3. Similarly, the slight decline in catalytic performance (ca. 20.0%) observed in simulated aqueous samples formulated from tap water was ascribed to the relatively high Cl− content, as quantified by ion chromatography (CIC-D160+, Qingdao Shenghan Chromatograph Technology Co., Ltd.) (Supplementary Table 7).

To identify the ROSs involved in the BUC-95/PDS/OFC system, quenching experiments were conducted using methanol (MeOH, for SO4•−), tert-butanol (TBA, for •OH), benzoquinone (BQ, for O2•−), nitrogen (N2, for O2•−), and L-histidine (L-his, for 1O2) as trapping agents11,26,27. The presence of these trapping agents led to slight inhibition (MeOH: 4.8% inhibition; TBA: 4.4% inhibition; L-his: 2.7% inhibition; BQ: 5.9% inhibition) of OFC degradation (Fig. 2g and Supplementary Fig. 30), demonstrating the negligible role of SO4•−, •OH, O2•−, and 1O2. Moreover, the electron spin resonance (ESR) results (Supplementary Fig. 31) revealed the presence of DMPO-SO4•−, DMPO-•OH, DMPO-O2•−, and TEMP-1O2 signals, indicating the formation of SO4•−, •OH, O2•−, and 1O2. Upon the addition of D2O, the TEMP-1O2 signal showed an obvious decrease (Supplementary Fig. 32a), a phenomenon attributable to solvent isotope and exchange effects between D2O and H2O28. To further evaluate the contribution of 1O2 in the BUC-95/PDS system, the OFC degradation experiment was conducted in D2O. Only slight declines in both OFC degradation efficiency (ca. 7.0%) and reaction rate (1.9 min−1) were observed (Supplementary Fig. 32b), indicating that 1O2 did not play a substantive role in OFC removal.

As probes of radicals, benzoic acid (BA) and 4-nitrobenzoic acid (NBA), which have low ESP values (Supplementary Fig. 33), slightly inhibited OFC removal. The degradation efficiencies of BA and NBA were only approximately 12.0% and 22.0%, respectively, further indicating the minor roles of SO4•− and •OH (Supplementary Fig. 34). While, the use of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), a high-valent iron-oxo (HVIO) scavenger, resulted in obvious inhibition (with a 23.57% decrease in removal efficiency) (Fig. 2g). This observation, coupled with the maintained catalytic activity under radical-suppressing conditions, strongly suggests that HVIO serves as the primary oxidative species rather than conventional ROSs.

Mechanistic insights into Fe(IV)=O formation
To investigate HVIO species formation, chemical trapping, Mössbauer spectroscopy and first-principles modeling were employed. HVIO species can oxidize methyl phenyl sulfoxide (PMSO) into methyl phenyl sulfone (PMSO2)29,30. PMSO oxidation tests revealed the production of 35.21 µM PMSO2 (6.4-fold increase compared to that of the individual PDS system), with a kobs of 0.31 min−1 (103-fold increase over that of the individual PDS system) using the BUC-95/PDS system (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 35). The 57Fe Mössbauer spectra of BUC-95 revealed a characteristic quadrupole splitting shift of −0.17 mm s−131,32, which is characteristic of the formation of HVIO species (Fig. 3b, c and Supplementary Table 8).

Typically, the formation of HVIO species can be attributed to both Fe(II) and Fe(III)33. Site masking experiments using 1,10-phenanthroline (phen, for Fe(II)) and KSCN (for Fe(III)) demonstrated that Fe(II) is the predominant precursor for HVIO formation, with OFC degradation inhibition rates of 29.03% and 86.03% following the addition of phen and KSCN, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 36). XPS quantification revealed a 15.78% decrease in the Fe(II) content after the reaction (Supplementary Fig. 37), which is generally consistent with the HVIO concentration (16.4%) determined via Mössbauer spectroscopy (Fig. 3d). Fluorobenzene (FB) was selected as the specific probe to determine the contribution of SO4•− to the HVIO formation because of its strong ability to coordinate with radicals. PMSO consumption (71.35 µM) significantly increased, whereas PMSO2 production (32.21 µM) did not obviously change in the BUC-95/PDS/FB system (Fig. 3a). These findings suggest that it is not the primary pathway for HVIO formation, highlighting a distinct pathway from conventional SO4•−-mediated ones34.

Previous literature reported that Fe sites, acting as the Lewis acid sites, can capture -OH from H2O to form Fe-OH species, which subsequently convert into HVIO species33,35. In BUC-95, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy revealed signals of oxygen vacancies at g = 2.003 (Supplementary Fig. 38), suggesting that oxygen vacancies may serve as favorable sites for Fe-OH formation. Further evidence comes from the O 1s XPS spectra, where a new peak emerges at 533.2 eV after reaction (Fig. 3e), consistent with the formation of Fe-OH species. These findings support a reaction mechanism in which HVIO generation is initiated by the adsorption of -OH from H2O onto Lewis acidic Fe(II) sites in BUC-95, forming Fe-OH intermediates that undergo a two-step oxygen atom transfer pathway to ultimately generate HVIO and SO42−.

Considering that HVIO species may exist as either Fe(IV)=O or Fe(V)=O, DFT calculations were conducted to identify the dominant HVIO species in the BUC-95-OH/PDS system36,37. A DFT model of BUC-95-OH/PDS was constructed, and the corresponding total adsorption energy for -OH and PDS was calculated as −9.61 eV, indicating that the HVIO formation spontaneous despite the presence of -OH groups (Fig. 3f). Bader charges from the two Fe sites to PDS and -OH were 1.6690 and 0.4823 (Fig. 3g), respectively, indicating that the -OH group in BUC-95 may facilitate partial charge transfer to support HVIO formation. This interpretation aligns with the observed reduction in electron density at the Fe site from 7.06 to 6.29 in the BUC-95-OH/PDS system (Supplementary Fig. 39). To assess the interaction between BUC-95-OH and PDS, the projected crystal orbital Hamilton population (pCOHP) was used. The calculated bond energies for Fe‒O (O from -OH) and Fe‒O (O from PDS) in the BUC-95-OH/PDS system were 1.82 eV and 2.00 eV, respectively, which are slightly lower than that of the Fe‒O bond in the BUC-95/PDS system (2.03 eV). This finding suggests that PDS is more readily desorbed during HVIO formation in the BUC-95-OH/PDS system (Fig. 3h).

More importantly, the critical roles of Fe and O orbitals and spin electrons in regulating Fe(IV)=O formation was strongly supported by projected density of states (PDOS) analysis (Supplementary Figs. 40–44). The splitting pattern of the Fe d orbitals undergoes significant changes upon adsorption of PDS and surficial -OH. This co-adsorption induces a transition in the crystal field splitting of Fe sites from tetrahedral to octahedral configuration, accompanied by a redistribution of electron density (Supplementary Fig. 45). Hybridization between the p orbitals of O atoms from PDS as well as -OH groups and the d orbitals of the Fe centers in BUC-95 lead to the formation of antibonding orbitals cross the Fermi level. As a result, two electrons from Fe dz2 orbitals are transferred to promote the formation of Fe(IV)=O species (Fig. 3i). The doublet peaks at pre-edge (ca. 528.0~535.0 eV) in O K-edge XAFS spectra revealed the feature of Fe 3d-O 2p hybridization (Fig. 3j). The reduced shaded area percentage (from 14.21% to 9.14%) and the decreased intensity of doublet peaks after reaction, verifying the intense hybridization between Fe 3d and O 2p orbitals, which supported the above results38,39. Thermodynamic profiling on the basis of the Gibbs free energy of the Fe(IV)=O formation process with and without -OH groups in BUC-95 demonstrated that BUC-95-OH exhibited a lower energy (−3.55 eV) than did BUC-95 (1.71 eV) in the rate-limiting step. This finding suggests that the energy barrier for Fe(IV)=O formation was markedly reduced in the presence of -OH groups (Fig. 3k).

Fe(IV)=O is recognized as a nonradical ROS with strong electrophilic properties and preferentially oxidizes electron-rich pollutants, as observed in highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy correlations40. The selective oxidation behavior of Fe(IV)=O in degrading the above mentioned electron-rich pollutants, such as ENR, NOR, CIP, TC, DCF, and electron-deficient pollutants, such as BA and NBA, was assessed by calculating their HOMO energy levels41. The HOMO values of ENR (−5.79 eV), NOR (−6.05 eV), CIP (−6.00 eV), TC (−6.16 eV), DCF (−6.14 eV) and OFC (−5.66 eV) were much higher than those of BA (−7.62 eV) and NBA (−8.23 eV) (Supplementary Fig. 46)42,43. These findings suggest that it is difficult for Fe(IV)=O to degrade electron-deficient pollutants, which is consistent with the results of the probing experiments.

Premixing experiments for BUC-95 and PDS at various time intervals (Supplementary Fig. 47), the open-circuit potential curves (Supplementary Fig. 48) and the i-t curve (Supplementary Fig. 49) excluded the contribution of the electron transfer process (ETP)44. The contributions of ROSs to OFC degradation were also assessed via probing experiments45,46. The contribution of Fe(IV)=O species to OFC degradation reached 85.6%, which was greater than those of SO4•− (8.0%) and •OH (6.4%) (Supplementary Fig. 50). Overall, based on the mechanism exploration of HVIO formation and OFC degradation, Fe(IV)=O species, rather than radicals, were recognized as the dominant ROSs in the BUC-95/PDS/OFC system (Fig. 3l), which aligned with the anion resistance and pH robustness results.

Significance of dynamic stretching on PDS activation
In contrast to conventional PDS activation paradigms that are governed primarily by electron transfer processes, electrochemical measurements revealed a distinct structure-activity difference of PDS activation between BUC-95 and BUC-96. The cyclic voltammetry (CV) profiles obtained for BUC-95 and BUC-96 after 20 cycles were recorded (Supplementary Fig. 51), and their corresponding double-layer capacitance (Cdl) values were calculated47. The Cdl of BUC-95 (9.05 mF cm−2) was lower than that of BUC-96 (9.10 mF cm−2), indicating that BUC-96 has a larger electrochemically active area for highly efficient PDS activation than does BUC-95 (Fig. 4a, b)48. The influence of the specific surface area of the as-synthesized samples on the above results was excluded (Supplementary Figs. 52 and 53 and Supplementary Table 9). Compared with that of BUC-95, a smaller electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) semicircle diameter was distinctly observed in BUC-96. This finding suggests that BUC-96 exhibits faster electron transfer efficiency (Fig. 4c). Meanwhile, post-reaction analysis revealed a more pronounced reduction in the Fe(Ⅱ) content was observed in BUC-96 (~17.54%) compared to BUC-95 (~15.78%), suggesting that BUC-96 exhibits stronger electron transfer and donating capabilities during PDS activation (Supplementary Fig. 54). However, BUC-96 did not exhibit satisfactory OFC degradation performance for PDS activation even with its superior electron transfer ability. This inverse correlation between electronic conductivity and reactivity underscores the critical role of flexible dynamic stretching, which influences more than just electron transfer in BUC-95.

To explore the significance of flexible dynamic stretching in the BUC-95/PDS system, comparative in situ PXRD tests of BUC-95 and BUC-96 under various environments were conducted. As shown in Fig. 4d, BUC-95 exhibited noticeable peak shifts in its PXRD patterns upon exposure to H2O and PDS, whereas BUC-96 maintained consistent diffraction peak positions under identical conditions. This contrast serves as direct evidence for the presence of flexible dynamic stretching in BUC-95. Additional confirmation was provided through in situ XPS, XAFS, FTIR and Raman characterizations. The Fe 2p3/2 peak in BUC-95 exhibited a clear binding energy shift (ca. 0.4 eV) with the addition of H2O and PDS (Supplementary Fig. 55a), in stark contrast to the minimal spectral variation (ca. 0.07 eV) observed in BUC-96 (Supplementary Fig. 55b). Meanwhile, in situ XANES analysis revealed that the absorption edge of pristine BUC-95 shifted toward higher energy upon water addition, with ΔE values of 0.14 eV and 0.28 eV after 1.0 min and 5.0 min, respectively. More obvious shifts (ΔE = 0.87 eV and 1.29 eV, respectively) were observed with the addition of PDS over the same time intervals. These energy shifts reflect structural changes induced by flexible dynamic stretching and an elevated oxidation state of Fe in BUC-95, consistent with the formation of Fe(IV)=O species (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 56).

Moreover, the in situ FTIR spectra of BUC-95 exhibited a red shift from 1395.94 cm−1 to 1392.41 cm−1 following the addition of PDS after 5.0 min of reaction (Fig. 4f). The Raman peaks at 708.6 cm−1 and 769.9 cm−1 for BUC-95 were attributed to Fe‒O and Fe‒N bonds. Upon introducing PDS into this reaction system, clear red shifts of the Fe‒O bond (from 708.6 cm−1 to 702.4 cm−1) and Fe‒N bond (from 769.9 cm−1 to 765.7 cm−1) were observed, indicating that the occurrence of large-scale and flexible dynamic change in BUC-95 may contribute to PDS activation (Fig. 4g). Moreover, PDS was consumed, with its initial concentration decreasing from 0.35 mM to 0.013 mM after the reaction, demonstrating successful PDS activation on the BUC-95 surface (Supplementary Fig. 57). After OFC was added to the above solution, all the Raman peaks returned to their original positions, and no new peaks were observed. Overall, the synergistic evidence from both crystallographic and electronic structure analyses conclusively indicates the presence of reversible and flexible dynamic stretching in BUC-95.

The homointerpenetrated framework of BUC-95 resulted in two geometrically distinct Fe coordination environments: (1) Dynamic dual-Fe sites (denoted Fe-Fe’), formed between two identically interpenetrated frameworks, exhibited interatomic distances ranging from 6.96 Å to 8.40 Å, as determined by microED (Supplementary Fig. 58); (2) Static and rigid dual-Fe sites (denoted Fe-Fe) confined within individual frameworks, displayed significantly shorter distances (3.82 Å) than did the Fe-Fe’ sites (Supplementary Fig. 59). Comparative analysis with the isostructural analog BUC-96 revealed structural convergence in both dynamic dual-Fe sites (denoted Fe-Fe”, ranging from 6.96 Å to 8.25 Å, Supplementary Fig. 60) and static sites (Fe-Fe in BUC-96 being 3.96 Å, static site Fe-Fe in BUC-95 being 3.82 Å; Supplementary Fig. 61). However, the flexible dynamic Fe-Fe’ configuration remained unique to BUC-95, as hydrogen bond in BUC-96 restricts such stretching within its interpenetrated framework. Importantly, the local coordination environments of Fe sites are identical in both MOFs (Supplementary Fig. 62), indicating that the enhanced PDS activation and OFC degradation in BUC-95 originate from its flexible dynamic stretching rather than differences in local metal coordination.

To investigate the role of structural dynamics on catalytic enhancement, comparative DFT calculations for BUC-95 and its analog BUC-96 were performed (Supplementary Fig. 63). Owing to their structural similarity, the adsorption energy of PDS on the Fe-Fe’ site in BUC-95 (−6.95 eV) and the corresponding O–O bond length (1.51 Å) closely match those in BUC-96 (−6.96 eV and 1.50 Å, respectively). This similarity indicates that PDS adsorption is not the primary factor driving the enhanced activation in BUC-95. Furthermore, Bader charge analysis reveals that electron transfer from the dynamic Fe-Fe’ sites to PDS is lower in BUC-95 (1.6437 e⁻) than that from the Fe-Fe” site in BUC-96 (1.6870 e⁻, Fig. 4h), suggesting that BUC-96 facilitates more efficient electron transfer, a conclusion consistent with electrochemical characterization.

Furthermore, PDOS analysis further reveals that the electron-occupied orbitals near the Fermi level (EF) in both BUC-95 and BUC-96 are governed primarily by Fe 3d, O 2p, and N 2p orbitals (Supplementary Figs. 64 and 65), consistent with Fe sites serving as the optimal PDS adsorption loci in both frameworks. To elucidate the role of dynamic structural flexibility, the electron distributions of the Fe 3d orbitals of BUC-95 and BUC-96 before and after PDS adsorption were compared (Fig. 4i). Upon PDS adsorption, the Fe 3d orbital area in BUC-96 undergoes a greater variation (Δarea = 0.74) than that in BUC-95 (Δarea = 0.04), indicating stronger electron transfer from BUC-96 to PDS and more effective electronic interaction at its Fe sites. These results were consistent with the Bader charge analysis, XAFS, and multiple electrochemical analyses.

Additionally, in situ molecular dynamics simulations under varied chemical environments and time resolutions (5.0, 10.0, 15.0, and 20.0 ps) confirm that BUC-95 exhibits clear reversible dynamic stretching in the presence of H2O and PDS (Fig. 4j and Supplementary Videos 2 and 3). In contrast, BUC-96 shows no significant structural change under the same condition (Supplementary Fig. 66 and Supplementary Videos 4-5). These findings further provide solid evidence for the unique, flexible dynamic stretching in the homointerpenetrated framework of BUC-95.

In summary, BUC-95 exhibited a weaker electron transfer ability in terms of PDS activation than BUC-96; however, its flexible dynamic stretching minimized the reliance on electron transfer efficiency, this mechanism significantly increased the Fenton-like catalytic efficiency, as evidenced by the excellent degradation performance (Supplementary Video 6).

Continuous-flow tests and toxicity assessment
To evaluate the practical applicability of the BUC-95/PDS system, a continuous-flow reactor was developed for the continuous and long-term removal of pollutants from pure water (Fig. 5a-b). BUC-95 was immobilized on a three-dimensional macroporous polyurethane sponge (2.0 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.0 cm) to construct a supported BUC-95@sponge (BS) catalyst. Polyvinyl butyral (PVB) was employed as a binder, providing satisfactory stability and flexibility (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 67). SEM images revealed that the rod-like BUC-95 was immobilized and uniformly distributed across the sponge. This finding was supported by EDS mapping, which verified the presence of Fe, N, O, and C (Fig. 5d). Compared with that of the blank sponge, the BS catalyst exhibited increased hydrophilicity, with a water contact angle of 54.85° (versus 113.97°) (Fig. 5b), facilitating interfacial contact between the catalyst, PDS, and pollutants. The hydraulic residence time was calculated to be 62.5 min. The BS/PDS system achieved >99.99% OFC (10.0 mg L−1) degradation efficiency within 110.0 h and maintained a high efficiency of >85% after 192.0 h in the simulated wastewater formulated by ultrapure water. In contrast, the individual PDS and PDS/sponge systems demonstrated negligible catalytic activity (~1.5% and ~1.9% degradation, respectively, Fig. 5e). Throughout the reaction, the BS catalyst exhibited high stability, with iron leaching concentrations remaining below <1.50 mg L−1, well under the limit specified by the Chinese National Standard (DB11/307–2013). SEM image (Supplementary Fig. 68) of the used BS after the reaction was identical to that of fresh BS, confirming its structural robustness and reusability. These results highlight the potential of the BUC-95 catalyst for scalable water treatment applications.

The degradation pathways of OFC in the BUC-95/PDS system were proposed on the basis of the Fukui index of OFC49 and ultra high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS) analysis results (Supplementary Figs. 69–72). The toxicity of OFC and its degradation intermediates was initially assessed via the Toxicity Estimation Software Tool (TEST) (Supplementary Fig. 73), along with plant and microorganism experiments. In the plant growth experiments, the root length, stem length, and growth status of mung beans in the degraded OFC solution obviously exceeded those in the undegraded OFC solution (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Fig. 74) because the BUC-95/PDS system not only effectively degrades organic pollutants but also ensures the generation of nontoxic intermediate products50,51. As depicted in Fig. 5g, the inhibition zone diameters measured in the blank solution (PBS), undegraded OFC solution, and degraded OFC solution at 10.0 min against E. coli were 8.0 mm, 22.0 mm and 10.0 mm, respectively, demonstrating the low/free toxicity of the OFC degradation products in the BUC-95/PDS system. These findings were confirmed by antibacterial experiments with multiple bacteria (Fig. 5h). By integrating high pollutant removal efficiency with effective detoxification and crop cultivation, the BUC-95/PDS system exhibited strong potential for practical applications in wastewater purification.

## Methods

Synthesis of BUC-95 and BUC-96
BUC-95 was prepared using FeSO4·7H2O (3.0 mmol), 4,4′-bipyridine (bpy, 3.0 mmol), and 1,4-benzenedicarboxylic acid (H2bdc, 3.0 mmol) dissolved in 45.0 mL of DMF and 20.0 mL of deionized water. The mixture was placed in a 250.0 mL reaction vessel and subjected to a microwave-assisted process (XH-100B, Xianghu Co., Beijing). The temperature of the mixture was raised to 106.0 °C within 2.0 min and held for 90.0 min, using a heating power of 700 W and a heating rate of 53.0 °C min−1. After the mixture had cooled to room temperature, the resulting crystals were collected through filtration and washed with deionized water. BUC-96 was synthesized following the same procedure, with the only difference being the replacement of H2bdc with 2,5-dihydroxyterephthalic acid (H4dhtp).

Detailed synthesis methods for other catalysts and the characterization techniques used are provided in Supplementary Notes 2–4.

Catalytic performance experiments
The degradation performance of different catalysis systems for OFC was evaluated using a PCX-50C reactor (Beijing Perfectlight Technology Co., Ltd.) with a stirring speed of 200.0 rpm operated at room temperature. In a typical setup, 0.2 g L−1 of catalyst was dispersed in 50.0 mL of OFC solution (10.0 mg L−1), and 0.35 mM of PDS was added to initiate the reaction. At specific intervals, 1.0 mL of reaction mixture was retrieved through a 0.22 µm membrane and injected into a vial containing 10.0 µL of methanol to terminate the catalytic reaction. The degradation kinetics were evaluated using a first-order rate equation: ln(Ct/C0) = −kt, where Ct, C0 and k are the residual concentration of pollutant at t min (mg L−1), initial concentration of pollutants (mg L−1) and degradation rate constant (min−1), respectively. The pH values were adjusted with H2SO4 or NaOH solutions. The methods used to analyze the residual concentrations of different pollutants are provided in Supplementary Note 5. All the experiments were carried out at least three times.

DFT calculation details
First-principles calculations based on DFT were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) in this work52. The exchange-correlation energy was treated using the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA)53. The BUC-95 model included a total of 260 atoms. Following tests for energy cut-off and k-point spacing tests, the energy was set to 300 eV, and a k-point spacing of 1×1×1 was used. The spin state was opened because of the presence of Fe, and the DFT+U approach was applied with a U value of 4.0 (d orbitals)54. The convergence standards for optimizing the crystal structure were <5.0×10−5 eV atom−1 (energy tolerance) and 0.05 eV Å−1 (maximum force tolerance). The specific calculation details are presented in Supplementary Note 10.

Q 3-6. MOFs are known for their high surface areas. However, the prepared BUC-95 and BUC-96 seem to have low specific surface areas. What are the reasons behind this?
Response 3-6: While high surface area is a hallmark feature of many metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), not all MOFs process a ultra-high specific surface area. The specific surface area of MOFs is influenced by some key factors like synthesis method, solvent selection, pore accessibility, and particle size.
First, MOFs synthesized by solvent/hydrothermal method generally exhibit high surface area. This is attributed to the extended synthesis time, which allows sufficient nucleation and growth periods, resulting in small pore sizes and a homogeneous distribution, thereby leading large specific surface areas. While, certain rapid MOF synthesis methods (microwave synthesis) involve short reaction times, which restrict adequate crystal growth. This causes structural defects in the framework that block the pores, preventing N (the probe for BET specific surface area testing) from entering and 2 thus resulting in a low specific surface area.
Additionally, if organic solvents (such as DMF or methanol) are used during MOF synthesis, these solvents may occupy the MOF's pores, resulting in the formation of small pore sizes and consequently reducing the specific surface area.
Last but not least, the size of MOF particles also significantly affects the specific surface area. In general, The specific surface area of MOF is related inversely to particle size. The smaller the particle size of MOF, the higher the specific surface area.

This unique structural feature enables reversible deformation of the entire framework in response to external stimuli like chemical activation. Unlike the localized pore breathing in conventional MOFs or the ligand-based flexibility in flexible MOFs (Supplementary Scheme 1), the large-scale dynamic adaptability of interpenetrated MOFs makes them ideal model systems for studying whole-framework dynamics in Fenton-like reaction mechanisms.

Interpenetrated MOFs are divided into two types: homointerpenetrated and heterointerpenetrated, which are formed by two independent MOF sub-frameworks interpenetrating each other to form an "interpenetrated structure" 1. Under external stimulation, reversible relative sliding/shifting occurs between the sub-frameworks, thereby achieving large-scale dynamic stretching of the whole framework 2. However, 29 it should be noted that after dynamic stretching, the topological structure of the sub- framework itself remains unchanged, and only its spatial position changes.
Flexible MOFs behavior refers to the reversible deformation (such as bending and compression) of a single MOF framework under external stimulation 3. However, it should be noted that its dynamic behavior originates from the adjustment of ligand conformation within a single framework, without synergy between multiple frameworks.
The ligand breathing effect of MOFs refers to the reversible contraction/expansion of pore size due to the local conformation of the ligand itself under external stimulation 4. However, the overall topological structure of the framework remains unchanged, and there is no collaboration between multiple frameworks.
In all, homointerpenetrated MOF is the "dynamic of multiple frameworks", flexible MOF is the "dynamic of a single framework", and ligand breathing effect of MOF is the "dynamic of pore" (Supplementary Scheme 1).

We therefore conclude that pore size effects do not contribute significantly to the observed catalytic performance.
